SHA-256 produces a fixed-size value from input of any length; it is not feasible to find two different inputs with the same value, so in practice changing the input changes the value.
claims.source_hint: FIPS 180-4 (Secure Hash Standard), SHA-256; .NET docs, System.Security.Cryptography.SHA256

claims.text: A digital signature is computed from a hash of the data with a private key; verification with the matching public key fails if the data changed or the signature was made with another private key.
claims.source_hint: FIPS 186-5 (Digital Signature Standard), ECDSA signature generation and verification; .NET docs, ECDsa.VerifyData

claims.text: At stage-1 the API signed JWTs with HMAC-SHA256 and one symmetric key that both creates and checks the signature, so any party able to check could also forge.
claims.source_hint: backend.l1.issuing-a-jwt five-line summary; backend.l2.validating-provider-tokens summary line 2; RFC 7518 section 3.2 (HMAC with SHA-2)

claims.text: A public key can verify a signature but cannot be used to create one. The check is only meaningful if the verifier holds the signer's real public key (how that is known: backend.l4.pki-and-signing).
claims.source_hint: glossary public-key; InvoiceSigning.cs @ stage-4 line 36 comment

claims.text: Non-repudiation holds only while the private key is held by the signer alone; a copied key lets anyone with the copy sign.
A signature does not encrypt or hide the signed data; the verifier needs the original bytes as they are.
claims.source_hint: .NET docs, ECDsa.VerifyData(byte[] data, byte[] signature, HashAlgorithmName) takes the plain data

claims.text: ToBytes serialises the invoice once with JsonSerializer.SerializeToUtf8Bytes and JsonSerializerOptions.Web; the comment says the bytes are kept with the signature because serialising again may not give the same bytes.
A different JsonSerializerOptions setting, such as WriteIndented, produces different bytes for the same object.
claims.source_hint: .NET docs, JsonSerializerOptions.WriteIndented; How to write .NET objects as JSON

claims.text: ECDsa.SignData(byte[], HashAlgorithmName) hashes the data with the given algorithm and signs the hash; VerifyData returns a bool (false on mismatch) rather than throwing.

ECDsa is the .NET class holding a key pair that makes and checks ECDSA signatures. Verify imports only the public key with ImportSubjectPublicKeyInfo; NewKey creates a P-256 pair in memory with ECDsa.Create(ECCurve.NamedCurves.nistP256), marked lab-only.
claims.source_hint: .NET 10 API reference, ECDsa class; ECDsa.Create(ECCurve), ECCurve.NamedCurves.nistP256, AsymmetricAlgorithm.ImportSubjectPublicKeyInfo; InvoiceSigning.cs lines 28-45

claims.text: InvoiceSigningTests: unchanged bytes verify with the public key alone (lines 15-22); replacing 2150000 with 2150001 makes Verify return false (24-34); a public key from another pair fails (36-44).
TLS protects data in transit on a connection; it leaves no proof in a saved file of who sent it or whether it was edited afterwards.
claims.source_hint: RFC 8446 section 1 (TLS goals: authentication, confidentiality, integrity of the channel)

claims.text: Trade-offs: a database row is enough while nobody outside must check; a shared HMAC key lets every checker also forge; a private-key signature alone gives an outsider an independent check, at the cost of a key pair and keeping signed bytes.
Choices: no signature when only Đơn Hàng's own pages show invoices; hand auditors the stored signed bytes, not a re-serialisation; a shared key can suffice when every checker is trusted to sign.
